On Friday 27 November I'm speaking at [AI & Marginalized Knowledge Systems](https://itatsulab.jp/2026/11/09/ai-marginalized-knowledge-systems/), a joint workshop of the Itatsu Lab at the University of Tokyo and the Center for Research and Practice in Cultural Continuity at the University of Warsaw, where I sit on the board. It's the second workshop under that name. The first was in Warsaw in June, where I gave [Who Governs the Spoken Word?](../2026-06-09-marginalized-knowledge-systems-warsaw/index.qmd)

My talk is "Who Speaks for Learners? Speech AI, Minoritized Languages and the Limits of EU Law."

Speech recognition and synthetic voices for minoritized languages are trained almost entirely on fluent adult speakers. That leaves out the people who actually keep these languages going: learners, children, new speakers. I look at the gap through two cases, Frisian in the Netherlands and Irish in AAC assistive technology. Then I turn to the law. EU AI law gives rights to individuals and duties to providers. A community harmed as a community has no clear remedy. That's the same problem I raised at [Ege University](../2026-11-04-standing-to-be-heard-ege-university/index.qmd) earlier this month, seen this time from the learner's side.

I'm in good company. Justyna Olko speaks on equity in digital tools built with Indigenous communities, Asuka Ando on collecting Japanese Sign Language data as a CODA researcher, Matthew Guay on AI for Yaeyaman, and Xinqi He on what large language models do to language itself.

The workshop is hybrid and runs 16:45–19:00 JST (08:45–11:00 in Amsterdam) at the Faculty of Engineering Building 2 on the Hongo campus. No registration needed. The Zoom link is on the [event page](https://itatsulab.jp/2026/11/09/ai-marginalized-knowledge-systems/).

Thanks to Yuko Itatsu and her lab for hosting.
